stem: Out of the following which is the Pythagorean triplet?
solution: A Pythagorean triplet satisfies (largest)\(^2\) = sum of squares of the other two. For \((3, 4, 5)\): \(3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2\). Hence \((3, 4, 5)\) is the Pythagorean triplet.

stem: Two circles of radii \(5.5\) cm and \(3.3\) cm respectively touch each other externally. What is the distance between their centres?
solution: For two circles touching externally, the distance between their centres equals the sum of their radii: \(5.5 + 3.3 = 8.8\) cm.

stem: Distance of point \((-3, 4)\) from the origin is ______.
solution: Distance from origin \(= \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: Find the volume of a cube of side \(3\) cm:
solution: Volume of a cube \(= (\text{side})^3 = 3^3 = 27\) cm\(^3\).

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: The ratio of corresponding sides of similar triangles is \(3 : 5\), then find the ratio of their areas.
solution:
The ratio of areas of two similar triangles equals the ratio of the squares of their corresponding sides.
\(\therefore\) Ratio of areas \(= 3^2 : 5^2 = 9 : 25\).

stem: Find the diagonal of a square whose side is \(10\) cm.
solution: Diagonal of a square \(= \sqrt{2} \times \text{side} = \sqrt{2} \times 10 = 10\sqrt{2}\) cm.

stem: \(\square ABCD\) is cyclic. If \(\angle B = 110^\circ\), then find measure of \(\angle D\).
solution:
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
\(\therefore \angle B + \angle D = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore 110^\circ + \angle D = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle D = 70^\circ\).

stem: Find the slope of the line passing through the points \(A(2, 3)\) and \(B(4, 7)\).
\(O\) is the centre of the circle, seg PS is a tangent segment and \(S\) is the point of contact. Line PR is a secant. If \(PQ = 3.6\), \(QR = 6.4\), find PS.
solution:
By the tangent secant segments theorem:
\(PS^2 = PQ \times PR\)
\(= PQ \times (PQ + QR)\)
\(= 3.6 \times (3.6 + 6.4)\)
\(= 3.6 \times 10\)
\(= 36\)
\(\therefore PS = 6\)  …(by taking square roots)
figureNote: Circle with centre O; external point P; tangent segment PS touching the circle at S; secant line PR through the circle cutting it at Q and R. (page 1)

stem: If \(\sec\theta = \dfrac{25}{7}\), find the value of \(\tan\theta\).
solution:
\(1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\)
\(\therefore 1 + \tan^2\theta = \left(\dfrac{25}{7}\right)^2\)
\(\therefore \tan^2\theta = \dfrac{625}{49} - 1 = \dfrac{625 - 49}{49} = \dfrac{576}{49}\)
\(\therefore \tan\theta = \dfrac{24}{7}\)  …(by taking square roots)

stem:
\(O\) is the centre of the circle. Points \(A\), \(B\), \(X\), \(Y\) lie on the circle with \(X\) on the minor side and \(Y\) on the major side of chord AB, and the central angle \(\angle AOB = 100^\circ\) (subtending arc AXB). Using the given information complete the following table:

| Type of arc | Name of the arc | Measure of the arc |
|---|---|---|
| Minor arc |  |  |
| Major arc |  |  |
solution:
The measure of a minor arc equals the measure of its corresponding central angle; the major arc is the rest of the circle.

| Type of arc | Name of the arc | Measure of the arc |
|---|---|---|
| Minor arc | arc AXB | \(100^\circ\) |
| Major arc | arc AYB | \(360^\circ - 100^\circ = 260^\circ\) |
figureNote: Circle with centre O; A and B on the circle with central angle 100° marked at O; X on the minor arc (bottom) and Y on the major arc (top). (page 1)

stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), \(NM \parallel RQ\). If \(PM = 15\), \(MQ = 10\), \(NR = 8\), then find PN.
solution:
In \(\triangle PQR\), \(NM \parallel RQ\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem:
\(\dfrac{PN}{NR} = \dfrac{PM}{MQ}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{PN}{8} = \dfrac{15}{10}\)
\(\therefore PN = \dfrac{15 \times 8}{10} = 12\).
figureNote: Triangle PQR with P at apex; N on side PR and M on side PQ; segment NM drawn parallel to base RQ. (page 1)

stem: In \(\triangle MNP\), \(\angle MNP = 90^\circ\), seg \(NQ \perp\) seg \(MP\). If \(MQ = 9\), \(QP = 4\), then find NQ.
solution:
By the theorem of geometric mean (right angle drawn perpendicular to the hypotenuse), \(NQ\) is the geometric mean of \(MQ\) and \(QP\):
\(NQ^2 = MQ \times QP = 9 \times 4 = 36\)
\(\therefore NQ = 6\).
figureNote: Right-angled triangle MNP with right angle at N; Q is the foot of the perpendicular from N to the hypotenuse MP. (page 1)

stem: \(M\) is the centre of the circle and seg KL is a tangent segment. \(L\) is a point of contact. If \(MK = 12\), \(KL = 6\sqrt{3}\), then find the radius of the circle.
solution:
The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact, so \(\angle MLK = 90^\circ\).
In right-angled \(\triangle MLK\), by Pythagoras theorem:
\(MK^2 = ML^2 + KL^2\)
\(\therefore 12^2 = ML^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2\)
\(\therefore 144 = ML^2 + 108\)
\(\therefore ML^2 = 36\)
\(\therefore ML = 6\)
The radius of the circle is \(6\).
figureNote: Circle with centre M; external point K; tangent segment KL touching the circle at L; radius ML and segment MK drawn. (page 2)

stem: Find the co-ordinates of midpoint of the segment joining the points \((22, 20)\) and \((0, 16)\).
solution: Midpoint \(= \left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{22 + 0}{2}, \dfrac{20 + 16}{2}\right) = (11, 18)\).

stem: A person is standing at a distance of \(80\) metres from a Church and looking at its top. The angle of elevation is of \(45^\circ\). Find the height of the Church.
solution:
Let the height of the Church be \(h\) metres. The horizontal distance is \(80\) m and the angle of elevation is \(45^\circ\).
\(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{h}{80}\)
\(\therefore 1 = \dfrac{h}{80}\)
\(\therefore h = 80\) metres.
The height of the Church is \(80\) m.

stem: In the given figure, \(X\) is any point in the interior of the triangle DEF. Point \(X\) is joined to the vertices of the triangle. seg \(PQ \parallel\) seg DE, seg \(QR \parallel\) seg EF (with \(P\) on XD, \(Q\) on XE, \(R\) on XF). Prove that seg \(PR \parallel\) seg DF.
solution:
Proof:
In \(\triangle XDE\),
\(PQ \parallel DE\)  …(Given)
\(\therefore \dfrac{XP}{PD} = \dfrac{XQ}{QE}\)  …(Basic proportionality theorem) …(i)
In \(\triangle XEF\),
\(QR \parallel EF\)  …(Given)
\(\therefore \dfrac{XQ}{QE} = \dfrac{XR}{RF}\)  …(Basic proportionality theorem) …(ii)
\(\therefore \dfrac{XP}{PD} = \dfrac{XR}{RF}\)  …[From (i) and (ii)]
\(\therefore\) seg \(PR \parallel\) seg DF  …(By converse of basic proportionality theorem)
figureNote: Triangle DEF (D top, E bottom-left, F bottom-right) with interior point X joined to all three vertices; P on XD, Q on XE, R on XF; inner triangle PQR drawn with PQ || DE and QR || EF. (page 2)

stem: If \(A(6, 1)\), \(B(8, 2)\), \(C(9, 4)\) and \(D(7, 3)\) are the vertices of \(\square ABCD\), show that \(\square ABCD\) is a parallelogram.
solution:
Slope of a line \(= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\)
\(\therefore\) Slope of line AB \(= \dfrac{2 - 1}{8 - 6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  …(i)
\(\therefore\) Slope of line BC \(= \dfrac{4 - 2}{9 - 8} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)  …(ii)
\(\therefore\) Slope of line CD \(= \dfrac{3 - 4}{7 - 9} = \dfrac{-1}{-2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  …(iii)
\(\therefore\) Slope of line DA \(= \dfrac{1 - 3}{6 - 7} = \dfrac{-2}{-1} = 2\)  …(iv)
Slope of line AB = Slope of line CD  …[From (i) and (iii)]
\(\therefore\) line AB \(\parallel\) line CD
Slope of line BC = Slope of line DA  …[From (ii) and (iv)]
\(\therefore\) line BC \(\parallel\) line DA
Both the pairs of opposite sides of the quadrilateral are parallel.
\(\therefore \square ABCD\) is a parallelogram.

stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), point \(S\) is the mid-point of side QR. If \(PQ = 11\), \(PR = 17\), \(PS = 13\), find QR.
solution:
\(S\) is the midpoint of QR, so PS is a median. By Apollonius theorem:
\(PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2\,PS^2 + 2\,SR^2\)
\(\therefore 11^2 + 17^2 = 2(13^2) + 2\,SR^2\)
\(\therefore 121 + 289 = 2(169) + 2\,SR^2\)
\(\therefore 410 = 338 + 2\,SR^2\)
\(\therefore 2\,SR^2 = 72\)
\(\therefore SR^2 = 36 \Rightarrow SR = 6\)
\(\therefore QR = 2 \times SR = 2 \times 6 = 12\).

stem: Prove that, tangent segments drawn from an external point to the circle are congruent.
solution:
Given: A circle with centre O. P is an external point. seg PA and seg PB are tangent segments touching the circle at A and B.
To prove: seg PA \(\cong\) seg PB.
Construction: Draw seg OA, seg OB and seg OP.
Proof: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
\(\therefore \angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ\).
In right-angled \(\triangle OAP\) and \(\triangle OBP\):
\(OA = OB\)  (radii of the same circle)
hypotenuse \(OP = OP\)  (common side)
\(\therefore \triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP\)  (Hypotenuse-side test)
\(\therefore PA = PB\)  (c.s.c.t.)
\(\therefore\) seg PA \(\cong\) seg PB.
Hence, tangent segments drawn from an external point to a circle are congruent.

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle with radius \(4.1\) cm. Construct tangents to the circle from a point at a distance \(7.3\) cm from the centre.
solution:
Steps of construction:
1. Draw a circle with centre O and radius \(4.1\) cm.
2. Take a point P such that \(OP = 7.3\) cm and draw seg OP.
3. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg OP; let it intersect OP at M (its midpoint).
4. With M as centre and radius MO (\(= MP = 3.65\) cm), draw a circle intersecting the given circle at points A and B.
5. Draw line PA and line PB.
Line PA and line PB are the required tangents to the circle from point P.
(Justification: \(\angle OAP\) and \(\angle OBP\) are angles in a semicircle, hence \(90^\circ\), so PA and PB are tangents.)

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: A metal cuboid of measures \(16\) cm \(\times\) \(11\) cm \(\times\) \(10\) cm was melted to make coins. How many coins were made, if the thickness and diameter of each coin was \(2\) mm and \(2\) cm respectively? \((\pi = 3.14)\)
solution:
Volume of the cuboid \(= 16 \times 11 \times 10 = 1760\) cm\(^3\).
Each coin is a cylinder with diameter \(2\) cm, so radius \(r = 1\) cm, and thickness (height) \(= 2\) mm \(= 0.2\) cm.
Volume of one coin \(= \pi r^2 h = 3.14 \times 1^2 \times 0.2 = 0.628\) cm\(^3\).
Number of coins \(= \dfrac{\text{Volume of cuboid}}{\text{Volume of one coin}} = \dfrac{1760}{0.628} \approx 2802\) coins.

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), PQ is a line segment intersecting AB at P and AC at Q such that seg \(PQ \parallel\) seg BC. If PQ divides \(\triangle ABC\) into two parts having equal areas, find \(\dfrac{BP}{AB}\).
solution:
Since \(PQ \parallel BC\), \(\triangle APQ \sim \triangle ABC\).
PQ divides \(\triangle ABC\) into two equal areas, so
\(A(\triangle APQ) = \dfrac{1}{2} A(\triangle ABC)\), i.e. \(\dfrac{A(\triangle APQ)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
By the theorem of areas of similar triangles:
\(\dfrac{A(\triangle APQ)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \left(\dfrac{AP}{AB}\right)^2\)
\(\therefore \left(\dfrac{AP}{AB}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{AP}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
Now \(\dfrac{BP}{AB} = \dfrac{AB - AP}{AB} = 1 - \dfrac{AP}{AB} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle of radius \(2.7\) cm and draw a chord PQ of length \(4.5\) cm. Draw tangents at points \(P\) and \(Q\) without using centre.
solution:
Steps of construction:
1. Draw a circle with centre O and radius \(2.7\) cm.
2. Draw a chord PQ of length \(4.5\) cm on the circle.
3. Take a point R on the major arc of the circle and draw seg PR and seg QR (to use the tangent–secant/inscribed-angle relation).
4. At point P, draw a ray PX such that \(\angle QPX = \angle PRQ\) (angle in the alternate segment); ray PX is the tangent at P.
5. Similarly, at point Q, draw a ray QY such that \(\angle PQY = \angle PRQ\); ray QY is the tangent at Q.
Lines through PX and QY are the required tangents at P and Q, drawn without using the centre (by the tangent–secant angle theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment).

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: \(\square ABCD\) is a square of side \(50\) m. Points \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\) are midpoints of side AB, side BC, side CD, side AD respectively. Find the area of the shaded region.
solution:
Side of the square \(= 50\) m, so area of square \(ABCD = 50 \times 50 = 2500\) m\(^2\).
At each corner of the square, a quarter circle is drawn with radius equal to half the side \(= 25\) m (joining the midpoints of the two sides at that corner). There are 4 such quarter circles, one at each corner.
Total area of the 4 quarter circles \(=\) area of 1 full circle of radius \(25\) m \(= \pi r^2 = 3.14 \times 25^2 = 3.14 \times 625 = 1962.5\) m\(^2\).
Area of shaded region \(=\) area of square \(-\) area of 4 quarter circles \(= 2500 - 1962.5 = 537.5\) m\(^2\).
figureNote: Square ABCD (A top-left, D top-right, C bottom-right, B bottom-left) of side 50 m; P, Q, R, S are midpoints of AB (left), BC (bottom), CD (right), AD (top); a concave four-pointed shaded star region with vertices at P, Q, R, S formed by four inward quarter-circle arcs centred at the corners. (page 3)

stem: Circles with centres \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) touch each other externally. If \(AB = 3\) cm, \(BC = 3\) cm, \(CA = 4\) cm, then find the radii of each circle.
solution:
Let the radii of the circles with centres A, B, C be \(r_A\), \(r_B\), \(r_C\). For externally touching circles, the distance between centres equals the sum of the radii:
\(r_A + r_B = AB = 3\)  …(i)
\(r_B + r_C = BC = 3\)  …(ii)
\(r_C + r_A = CA = 4\)  …(iii)
Adding (i), (ii), (iii): \(2(r_A + r_B + r_C) = 10 \Rightarrow r_A + r_B + r_C = 5\)  …(iv)
From (iv) and (i): \(r_C = 5 - 3 = 2\) cm.
From (iv) and (ii): \(r_A = 5 - 3 = 2\) cm.
From (iv) and (iii): \(r_B = 5 - 4 = 1\) cm.
\(\therefore r_A = 2\) cm, \(r_B = 1\) cm, \(r_C = 2\) cm.

stem: If \(\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\), show that: \(\cos^2\theta + \cos^4\theta = 1\).
solution:
Given: \(\sin\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\)
\(\therefore \sin\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\)  …(i)  (since \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\))
Now consider the L.H.S.:
\(\cos^2\theta + \cos^4\theta = \cos^2\theta + (\cos^2\theta)^2\)
\(= \sin\theta + (\sin\theta)^2\)  …[from (i), \(\cos^2\theta = \sin\theta\)]
\(= \sin\theta + \sin^2\theta\)
\(= 1\)  …(given)
\(\therefore \cos^2\theta + \cos^4\theta = 1\).
